name: Grow & keep
desc: A vegetable patch, pots on a balcony, easy crops, sprouts, potatoes, saving seeds, compost, drying, pickling and storing

s: Pick the sunniest spot you have: vegetables need at least 6 hours of sun a day.
Keep the bed about 1.2 metres wide, so you can reach the middle from both sides without stepping on the soil.
Remove grass and weeds, loosen the soil a spade deep and mix in a few buckets of compost.
Start small: one bed you look after well gives more than three you can't keep up with.
Water the soil, not the leaves, early in the morning. Once deep is better than a little every day.
Cover bare soil between the plants with straw, grass clippings or leaves: it keeps the water in and the weeds out.
d: Don't sow frost-tender plants (beans, courgettes, tomatoes) outside before mid-May in the Netherlands

guides.t: Growing in pots on a balcony
s: Use pots with holes in the bottom. Bigger is easier: 10 litres for lettuce and herbs, 20 litres or more for a tomato or courgette.
Fill them with potting compost from a garden centre, not garden soil: it stays light and drains better.
Easy winners: herbs, lettuce, rocket, radishes, cherry tomatoes, dwarf beans, strawberries and chillies.
In summer pots dry out fast: water every day, twice in a heatwave, until it runs out of the bottom.
Once plants flower, feed them every 1–2 weeks with liquid plant food (tomato feed works for most).
Shelter them from strong wind, and turn the pots now and then so they grow straight.
d: Don't let pots stand in a saucer full of water for days: the roots rot

s: Radishes: sow straight into the soil, ready in about 4 weeks.
Lettuce and rocket: pick the outer leaves and they keep growing for weeks (cut-and-come-again).
Courgettes: one or two plants feed a family all summer. Pick them small and often.
Dwarf beans and peas: sow in the soil once it's warm; pick often and they make more.
Kale and chard: keep going into winter, even in Dutch frost.
Potatoes: one of the most food for the space, and they store for months (see Growing potatoes).
Sow little and often (every 2–3 weeks) so not everything is ready on the same day.

guides.w: Fresh food in 4 days, no garden
s: Use seeds sold for sprouting: mung beans, lentils, alfalfa, broccoli or radish seeds.
Put 2 tablespoons in a clean glass jar, cover with water and soak overnight.
Cover the jar with a cloth or mesh held by an elastic band, pour the water out and rinse with clean water.
Rinse and drain twice a day, leaving the jar upside down at an angle so it drains.
After 3–5 days they're ready. Rinse, dry and keep them cool; eat within 2 days.
For young children, pregnant or elderly people, cook sprouts before eating.
d: Don't sprout raw kidney beans: they're poisonous unless boiled hard
Throw them out if they smell bad or look slimy

guides.w: The most food for the space
s: Use seed potatoes, or shop potatoes that have sprouted. Let them sprout in a light, cool place for a few weeks first.
Plant them about 10 cm deep and 30 cm apart, sprouts pointing up. In the Netherlands: April; in Puglia: from February.
When the plants are about 20 cm tall, pull soil up around the stems (earthing up). Do it again a few weeks later.
Water in dry weather, especially when the plants flower.
New potatoes: dig carefully when the plants flower. Storing potatoes: wait until the leaves die back.
Let them dry on the soil for a few hours, then store them dark, cool and dry (see Storing a harvest).
d: Don't eat green potatoes or the leaves and berries of the plant: they're poisonous

s: Start with easy ones: beans, peas, tomatoes, lettuce and chillies.
Beans and peas: leave some pods on the plant until they're dry and rattle, then shell them.
Tomatoes: squeeze the seeds with their jelly into a glass with a little water. Leave 2–3 days until it smells, rinse in a sieve and dry on a plate.
Dry all seeds completely for a week or two, spread out, out of the sun.
Keep them in paper envelopes, labelled with the plant and the year, in a cool, dark, dry place.
Most seeds stay good for 2–4 years.
d: Seeds from F1 (hybrid) varieties don't grow true: the next plants can be very different

s: Mix roughly half “greens” (vegetable peels, coffee grounds, grass clippings) and half “browns” (dry leaves, cardboard, straw).
Chop big pieces smaller: they rot faster.
Keep it as damp as a wrung-out sponge: water it in dry weather, add browns if it's wet and smelly.
Turn it with a fork every few weeks to get air in.
After 6–12 months it's dark and crumbly: that's compost. Use it on your beds and in pots.
d: No meat, fish, dairy or cooked food: it attracts rats
No diseased plants or weeds with seeds

guides.w: Keeps for months without a fridge
s: Slice fruit or vegetables thinly and evenly (about 5 mm). Apples, pears, tomatoes, mushrooms and herbs work well.
Lay the slices on a rack or tray with space between them, so air can get around.
Dry them in warm, dry, moving air: in hot sun covered with a cloth against insects, near a stove, or in an oven at its lowest heat with the door open a crack.
Fruit is ready when it's leathery and no juice comes out when you squeeze it; vegetables when they're brittle.
Herbs: hang small bunches upside down in a dry, airy place.
Store in airtight jars. Check after a few days: any moisture inside means dry them longer.
d: Throw away anything that grows mould
guides.src: Food-preservation guidance (USDA National Center for Home Food Preservation)

s: Quick pickles: heat equal parts vinegar and water with a spoon of salt and a spoon of sugar per half litre. Pour it hot over sliced vegetables in a clean jar. Keep in the fridge and eat within a few weeks.
Sauerkraut: weigh shredded cabbage and add 2% salt (20 g per kilo). Squeeze and knead it until it gives off liquid.
Press it tightly into a clean jar until the liquid covers it. Keep everything under the liquid with a weight (a small bag of water works).
Leave it at room temperature for 1–4 weeks, opening the lid daily to let gas out. Taste it: when you like the sourness, move it somewhere cool.
A white film on top can be skimmed off.
d: Throw it away if there's fuzzy, coloured mould or it smells rotten
Don't store vegetables, garlic or herbs in oil at room temperature: risk of botulism
guides.src: Food-preservation guidance (USDA National Center for Home Food Preservation)

s: Potatoes: dark, cool (4–8 °C) and dry, in paper or cloth sacks. Light turns them green.
Onions and garlic: dry them in the sun for a week, then hang them in a dry, airy place.
Pumpkins and squash: let the skin harden in the sun, then keep them at room temperature: they last for months.
Apples: wrap each one in paper and keep them cool, away from potatoes (they make each other go off faster).
Carrots and beetroot: in a box of damp sand in a cool shed or cellar.
Check everything every week and remove anything going soft: one bad one spoils the rest.
